Safety Briefing — Port Melbourne
Safety Briefing

Port Melbourne

This page assembles the briefing. It doesn't make the call. The on-water risk assessment and the go / no-go rest with the activity leader and the sailor — read it, read the day, and decide.

Today's inputs all feeds live

Wind, gust, direction and air temperature from the Bay Winds stations; UV, sun/cloud, rain and forecast from Open-Meteo; tide from the Bureau's observed gauge at St Kilda Marina (next turn predicted); water temp from NOAA satellite SST. Every field is live — the controls are fallbacks, and for testing.

Today, on the water

connecting…

Weather

Temperature, wind, tide and what they mean for the crew.

Read the wind, the tide and the change before you launch. Match clothing, sun cover and wetsuits to the day.

Cold and heat: the crew check each other, not only the instructor — the one affected is the last to notice.

  • Cold: shivering that won't stop → off the water and warm up. Shivering stopping while still cold is worse, not better.
  • Heat: confusion, stumbling, or skin that's stopped sweating → Triple Zero (000) and cool fast.
  • In doubt either way, head in.

Full signs and steps on the Cold & Heat page.

Water quality: stormwater after rain lifts the bacteria count — hold off immersion a day or two after heavy rain, worse near drains and the pier outfalls. Check EPA's water-quality and incident map for Port Melbourne.

The guiding line for the PMYC area: stay in direct sight of the PMYC Tower. If the Tower can't see you, you've gone too far.

PMYC to Black Rock is about 15 km in a straight line, some 16 km along the shore. Plan the run on this chart; sail each leg on its area chart.

St Kilda is open-water passage, not the triangle. Red water is no-vessel water. Give the breakwater a wide berth — penguins, no access — and keep clear of the two isolated-danger marks. Back before dark, unless it's the planned twilight sail.

Crossing to Williamstown means crossing the port's shipping channels. Ships can't stop or turn for you, and they sometimes run outside the fairways. Cross at right angles, keep moving, and never stop in a channel.

Williamstown is a working harbour. Come in slowly, keep clear of the dredged channel off the pier ends, and expect power boats and commercial traffic around the piers.

Port Melbourne to St Kilda runs along the beaches. Stay out of the red, stay east of the Port of Melbourne limit, and keep clear of the two isolated-danger marks.

St Kilda to Brighton is about 5 km of open water down the eastern shore. Stay out of the red and well east of the shipping channel.

Brighton to Black Rock is about 7 km along the shore, with Sandringham's harbour halfway. Stay out of the red, keep clear of the marks off Sandringham and in Half Moon Bay, and don't anchor in the pink band offshore.

Half Moon Bay is sheltered water with hard edges: no-vessel zones, a protected wreck and two cardinals offshore. Keep out of the red, keep well clear of Cerberus, and pass outside the cardinals.

Sandringham to Mount Martha is about 35 km of open shore. There are harbours along the way — plan which one you'd use before you need it.

Mornington to Dromana is about 15 km along the shore, past Mount Martha and Martha Cove to Safety Beach.

Dromana to Point Nepean is about 28 km along the southern shore, with the South Channel's ships close offshore the whole way.

This is the Heads' doorstep. Know where the designated hazardous area starts, keep clear of the South and Coles channels, and don't land at Point Nepean.

The guide is plain: the Rip can be quite difficult — strong tidal movements, large and unpredictable waves, and frequent shipping. Seek quality advice before attempting to pass through.

Queenscliff to Geelong is some 40 km round the Bellarine shore, past St Leonards, Indented Head, Portarlington and Clifton Springs into Corio Bay.

Geelong to Point Cook is about 45 km, out of Corio Bay past Avalon and Point Wilson, then north-east along Werribee South.

Point Cook to St Kilda is about 17 km, across Altona Bay and past Williamstown, then over the shipping channels to Port Melbourne.

St Kilda to Geelong is about 60 km of open water. Treat it as a passage: weather, daylight, and a harbour you could reach on either shore.

Some 1,950 km² of water, with two shipping routes — in through the Heads and up to Port Melbourne, and through Corio Bay to Geelong. Plan here; sail it on the area charts.

The area & the launch

  • The triangle: Station Pier — Lagoon Pier — the G marker. Depth about 2–5 m.
  • Launch from the east beach by the club (the Dog Beach) — the shared 5-knot zone, and no access lane, so 5 knots the whole way to 200 m. Stay clear of the Port Melbourne lifesaving-club swim-only zone.
  • Sandbank 20–30 m out: seen at high tide, barely covered at low. Wade the boat onto / past it to launch; head into the wind just short of it to land. Don't copy the cat sailors up the sand.

The piers

  • Lagoon Pier (ESE): wide berth. The stormwater drain ~100 m short is the turn-back line. Fishing lines; kids jumping.
  • Station Pier (W): keep 50 m and well clear of a berthed ship — check today against the cruise-ship schedule (the east berth is “OESP”).

Traffic, marks & wildlife

  • Jet skis are the number-one hazard, even in the 5-knot band. Swimmers, SUPs, dogs on the Dog Beach, anchored fishing boats between club and G marker, water police.
  • The G marker is a race mark for the big clubs — leave it when a yacht fleet is heading for it.
  • Dolphins on flat northerly mornings; jellyfish in season.

The whole run

  • Legs: PMYC to St Kilda Pier about 3.6 km; on to Middle Brighton Pier about 5 km; on to Black Rock Jetty about 7 km.
  • Shelter on the way: St Kilda harbour (RMYS), Middle Brighton (RBYC), Sandringham harbour (SYC) and Half Moon Bay (BRYC).
  • Keep east of the shipping channel and out of the inner anchorage; don't anchor in the prohibited anchorage zone over the gas pipeline.
  • Hazards near the shore: isolated dangers off Middle Park, St Kilda and Sandringham; cardinal marks off Brighton, in Half Moon Bay and at Black Rock Jetty; the protected wreck HMVS Cerberus at Black Rock.
  • Fawkner Beacon (Fl.5s17m), offshore from Sandringham, is one of the briefing's two wind stations; the other is RMYS.

The passage & the penguins

  • Open water the whole way down from the triangle, no shelter — treat it as a passage. Keep the group together and keep a line back to Port Melbourne.
  • Red is swimming only — no vessels: off Middle Park, and from the pier down to the marina. Crossed yellow poles mark its seaward edge; angled yellow buoys run along the orange shared-windsports zone.
  • The gaps between the zones — the top of Middle Park beach, the slipway beside the pier, the spit by the marina — aren't zoned, but they sit inside the 5-knot zone.
  • Two isolated-danger marks, black and red with twin black balls: Fl.(2)6s off Middle Park and Fl.(2)10s off the pier. Each marks a hazard at the mark itself — keep well clear.
  • The breakwater is little-penguin habitat — no access. Its head carries a green light (Fl.G.5s6m), with a yellow light (Fl.Y.5s) on the spur.
  • St Kilda Marina: red and green beacons and a fixed light (F.) on the spit mark the entrance. The south-cardinal (VQ(6)+Fl.(2)10s) off it to the west is passed on its south side. The hatched channel is boating only — no swimming. Fuel and a ramp are there if the power boat needs them.
  • Back before dark — the twilight sail to the penguins is a separate plan with its own night briefing.

The crossing & the ships

  • About 3.4 km from PMYC to Gem Pier, across two channels: the commercial shipping channel south of Station Pier, and the Williamstown channel with its swing basins.
  • Keep clear of ships at all times. Never obstruct one or assume it can see you — a ship's blind spot can run for hundreds of metres (the guide, p. 8).
  • Never anchor in a shipping channel or the Transit Only Lane, and never tie up to a navigation mark.
  • Swing basins (dashed circles) are where ships turn into and out of their berths — steer clear of them.
  • Look both ways up the channel before you commit, then cross at right angles and keep the group together.
  • Williamstown: the Royal Yacht Club of Victoria is at Gem Pier, Hobsons Bay Yacht Club to its north-west. The harbour chart has the piers in detail.

The piers & the channel

  • Pier-end lights, west to east: F.G on Ferguson St Pier, F.R on Gem Pier, F. on Workshops Jetty, F.G on Ann St Pier, Q. on Reid St Pier, F. on Nelson Pier West, F.R on Dockyard Pier, F. on Gellibrand Pier, Fl.R.2s on Breakwater Pier.
  • The dredged channel runs past the ends of Gellibrand and Breakwater piers — ships pass close there.
  • Inside the piers it's 5 knots; the water among the eastern piers is restricted area.
  • RYCV is at Gem Pier, HBYC to its north-west; fuel by Gem Pier.

The beaches & the marks

  • About 3.6 km from PMYC to St Kilda Pier, past Lagoon Pier, Kerferd Road Pier and Middle Park.
  • Red is swimming only — no vessels: off Albert Park and Middle Park. Crossed yellow poles mark the seaward edges.
  • Orange north of St Kilda Pier is shared windsports — other boats may use it within the speed and distance rules (the guide, p. 6).
  • 5 knots within 200 m of the shore, and within 50 m of a person, vessel or pier.
  • Isolated dangers, black and red with twin balls: Fl.(2)6s off Middle Park and Fl.(2)10s off St Kilda Pier — keep well clear.
  • The commercial shipping channel runs south from Station Pier — stay east of the Port of Melbourne limit.

The passage

  • About 5 km from St Kilda Pier to Middle Brighton Pier, with no shelter in between. Keep the group together.
  • Swimming-only zones off St Kilda and Elwood; the 5-knot zone runs the length of the shore.
  • Elwood Sailing Club is on the beach at Elwood, with green beacons along the shore there.
  • Middle Brighton Pier and its breakwater shelter RBYC's harbour; the light off the pier end is Fl.G.5s.
  • Isolated dangers off St Kilda — black and red with twin balls — keep clear.
  • Lit yellow buoys offshore are special marks; further out lies the shipping channel.

The passage

  • About 7 km from Middle Brighton Pier to Black Rock Jetty. Sandringham Yacht Club's harbour is the shelter halfway.
  • Swimming-only zones off Brighton, Hampton, Sandringham and Black Rock; shared windsports at Brighton and Hampton.
  • Off Sandringham, an isolated danger — keep clear. In Half Moon Bay, a west cardinal and an east cardinal: pass west of the first or east of the second, not between them.
  • The pink band offshore is a prohibited anchorage zone over the gas pipeline — don't anchor in it.
  • HMVS Cerberus, off Black Rock, is a protected wreck — keep out. The Sandringham to Black Rock chart has the detail.

The bay & the wreck

  • Sandringham Yacht Club's harbour beside Hampton Pier: entrance lights Q.R and Q.G, with Fl.(2)G.5s off the entrance; fuel and pump-out there.
  • Swimming-only zones off Hampton, Sandringham, the south shore of Half Moon Bay and Black Rock; shared windsports at Hampton.
  • Off Sandringham, an isolated danger (Fl.(2)10s) — keep clear.
  • Offshore in the bay, a west cardinal (VQ(9)10s) and an east cardinal (VQ(3)5s): pass west of the first or east of the second — not between them.
  • HMVS Cerberus is a protected wreck. It is illegal to enter its zone without a Heritage Victoria permit (the guide, p. 7). Pass west of the west cardinal off Black Rock Jetty.
  • BRYC sails off the beach on Cerberus Way, at the south end of the bay; 5 knots inshore.

The passage

  • About 35 km in a straight line, south-east past Beaumaris, Mordialloc, Carrum and Frankston, then south to Mount Martha.
  • Harbours on the way: Mordialloc Creek, the Patterson River at Carrum, Frankston and Mornington.
  • Off Beaumaris: Ricketts Point Marine Sanctuary, and further out the prohibited anchorage zone over the gas pipeline — don't anchor in it.
  • Off Frankston and Mount Eliza: an isolated danger and cardinal marks — keep clear, and pass each cardinal on its named side.
  • Swimming-only zones and swim-zone marks line the beaches; 5 knots within 200 m of the shore.

The passage

  • About 15 km from Mornington harbour to Dromana Pier.
  • Off Mornington: a west cardinal (VQ(9)10s) — pass west of it.
  • Martha Cove's marina entrance comes near the end of the run, with Safety Beach and Dromana Pier beyond.
  • Yellow special marks lie off Fishermans Bay and Mount Martha; the spoil ground offshore is outlined in dashes.
  • Swimming-only zones at Mornington, Mount Martha and Safety Beach; a waterski access lane at McCrae.

The passage

  • About 22 km from Dromana Pier to Portsea Pier, and some 6 km more to Point Nepean.
  • The South Channel carries the ships into the bay. Keep clear of ships at all times and never anchor in the channel.
  • Piers at Dromana, Rosebud, Rye, Sorrento and Portsea; Blairgowrie Safe Harbour (BYS) between Rye and Sorrento.
  • From Portsea west you're in Port Phillip Heads Marine National Park and nearing the designated hazardous area — see the Heads chart.
  • Swimming-only zones and swim-zone marks line the beaches; 5 knots within 200 m of the shore.

The southern bay

  • About 10 km across from Sorrento to Queenscliff, just inside the Heads; the car ferry runs between them.
  • The orange line marks the designated hazardous area of the Heads — lifejacket wear is mandatory in it, as the guide marks.
  • Port Phillip Heads Marine National Park (blue) takes in Swan Bay, Mud Islands, Popes Eye, Point Lonsdale and Point Nepean. Vessels are prohibited from landing at Point Nepean.
  • The South Channel and Coles Channel carry the ships; the prohibited anchorage zone lies off Point Lonsdale. Keep clear of ships.
  • Swan Island is restricted naval water.
  • St Leonards Jetty and Queenscliff are the harbours on the Bellarine side; Sorrento and Portsea on the peninsula.

The Heads

  • Port Phillip Heads is a designated hazardous area; lifejacket wear is mandatory there.
  • Vessels are prohibited from landing at Point Nepean, within Port Phillip Heads Marine National Park.
  • Ships use the channel through the Heads at all hours — keep clear of them, and never anchor in a channel.
  • Swan Island is restricted naval water; the prohibited anchorage zone lies off Point Lonsdale.
  • Protected wrecks — Clarence, Joanna, William Salthouse — keep out without a Heritage Victoria permit (the guide, p. 7).

The passage

  • North from Queenscliff past St Leonards and Indented Head, then west past Portarlington and Clifton Springs to Geelong.
  • Geelong's shipping channel runs through Corio Bay, edged by red and green marks — keep clear of ships and never anchor in it.
  • Across Corio Bay, Point Wilson is a restricted area — keep outside it.
  • Spoil grounds, outlined in dashes, lie off the Bellarine shore and in Corio Bay.
  • RGYC is on the Geelong waterfront.

The passage

  • About 45 km in a straight line from Geelong to Point Cook.
  • Out of Corio Bay, keep clear of the shipping channel and its ships.
  • Point Wilson is a restricted area — keep outside it.
  • Werribee South and the Werribee River offer shelter; Point Cooke Marine Sanctuary lies off Point Cook.
  • Spoil grounds lie offshore, outlined in dashes.

The passage

  • About 17 km in a straight line from Point Cook to St Kilda.
  • Point Cooke and Jawbone marine sanctuaries sit at either end of Altona Bay.
  • Altona Pier and Altona YC, then Williamstown — RYCV and HBYC.
  • Crossing to Port Melbourne means crossing the shipping channels — see the Williamstown crossing chart. Keep clear of ships and the inner anchorage.

The crossing

  • About 60 km in a straight line from St Kilda to Geelong.
  • You cross the shipping channel that runs south from Port Melbourne, and pass the anchorages — keep clear of ships, cross at right angles and keep moving.
  • Geelong's approach is through Corio Bay along its own shipping channel.
  • Off Avalon, Point Wilson is a restricted area; spoil grounds are outlined offshore.
  • Harbours on the way: Williamstown and Werribee South on the north shore, Portarlington and St Leonards on the Bellarine.

The bay

  • The Heads are a designated hazardous area, inside Port Phillip Heads Marine National Park.
  • Ships use the channels at all hours and sometimes run outside the fairways — keep clear of them at all times (the guide, p. 8).
  • Restricted areas: Point Wilson, Swan Island and the waters around the port channels; prohibited anchorage zones over the gas pipelines.
  • Every shore has its 5-knot zone and swimming-only stretches; the area charts carry them in detail.

Time

Set and spoken on the day.

  • Start and end.
  • Plan summary.
  • Boat allocations and roles.

Current time is in the header.

Communication

Signals, and the one that overrides everything.

  • Help — one fist overhead, or two fists overhead.
  • Attention, come closer — a low one-hand wave.
  • Fun — any other wave, with a happy face.

Return To Shore (RTS)

From the power boat: whistle, shout, November flag. Every boat returns on its own — shortest and safest way the captain judges. Don't wait for a further signal. Any beach will do, through a swim zone or beyond Lagoon Pier if needed; ideally the club launch. Regroup on the beach.

Radio: VHF generally CH 73.

Safety

Buddy system, capsize, first aid, head knocks.

Buddy system & counting

No one alone, ashore or afloat. The fleet looks after itself and stays together. X3s: small, orange stripe, 1–4 of them. Quest: bigger, white mast float, green accents, only one. Count before, count often, spot the gap — everyone's job.

Capsize drill

Reviewed on land each time. The three to remember:

  • Stay calm.
  • Is everyone OK?
  • Hold on to the boat.

Then: bow to wind, weight on the centreboard, take control, collect crew, set lines, sail on. Several boats over at once — stay calm, stay out of the water if you can, wait; someone will come.

First aid

Notify the safety boat first — it radios ahead. Kits: clubhouse upstairs by the tower stairs, and the boat shed by the sailing-school shed. Log what's used; incident report usually needed. Small cut, help yourself; anything real, get assistance.

Head knocks — concussion

A knock to the head doesn't always show at once, and the one hit is the worst judge of it — so the crew watches.

  • Knocked out, even for a second → Triple Zero (000); treat the neck as injured too.
  • A hard knock → come in and sit it out; don't sail on to test it.
  • A light bump → keep an eye out; it can come on over hours.

If in doubt, stay ashore or head back in — rest, and keep watching. The graded response and signs are on the Concussion page.
